summary: Starts a discussion about moving WAIS technology from Z39.50-1988 to Z39.50-1992 and then to Z39.50-1994. It is informational.

eli5.summary: WAIS is an old way to search libraries. This note starts a talk about upgrading it to newer versions.

questions: why use z39.50 for information retrieval
subtitle: The WAIS protocol implementation built on Z39.50-1988 information retrieval standard.

tldr.problem: Organizations wanted an open-architecture system for searching and publishing information across computer networks, but existing standards were designed for bibliographic data and assumed complex query capabilities.
tldr.mechanism: WAIS implemented Z39.50-1988 with a simpler text-based query system (Type-3 queries) instead of structured queries, a stateless server architecture, and document retrieval using relevance-ranked results.
tldr.outcome: WAIS became a widely-used network publishing system with over 50,000 Internet users by 1994, demonstrating that standards-based information retrieval could serve non-bibliographic data and diverse document formats.

today: RFC 1625 is an Informational RFC from 1994 documenting WAIS's architecture and design choices. WAIS was largely superseded by the World Wide Web and search engines (Google, etc.) in the late 1990s, though Z39.50 continues to be used in library systems and specialized information retrieval applications.

sections.title: Wide Area Information Servers
sections.content:
WAIS (Wide Area Information Servers) was designed in the late 1980s to help users find and retrieve information across computer networks. The system consists of four main components: the client (user interface), the server (runs on the machine hosting databases), the database (the information source), and the protocol (Z39.50-1988, the communication standard). WAIS development began in October 1989 with the first Internet release in April 1991. By the time this memo was written in 1994, over 50,000 users were using WAIS clients and servers connected via Z39.50-1988.

The WAIS project was guided by four key principles: creating a wide-area networked information system, building on published standards rather than proprietary protocols, designing for ease of use for non-technical users, and supporting growth and flexibility. To meet these goals, WAIS developers worked closely with the Z39.50 Implementors Group (ZIG) to use a recommended subset of the Z39.50-1988 standard with specific assumptions.
sections.eli5: WAIS is a networked search system that helps people find documents. Started in 1989, by 1994 it had tens of thousands of users, all using the same standard protocol to search different databases.

sections.title: Design Goals and Simplifications
sections.content:
WAIS had to adapt Z39.50, a standard designed for librarians searching bibliographic databases, to serve non-bibliographic information in diverse formats (text, images, PostScript, GIF). The designers made several key simplifications. Instead of requiring users or clients to know the Z39.50 Attributes supported by each server, WAIS clients sent simple Type-3 queries containing plain text entered by the user. The server handled parsing and attribute mapping internally. This meant clients did not need modification when server functionality changed.

WAIS servers were designed as stateless, deleting search result sets immediately after returning them rather than keeping them on the server. Retrieval was done using the Search Facility instead of the separate Present Facility. WAIS also supported relevance feedback, allowing users to select a document or document portion and find similar documents. To support large documents, clients could retrieve documents in chunks by specifying byte, line, or paragraph boundaries.
sections.eli5: WAIS made Z39.50 easier to use by hiding technical details from the user. Instead of learning special commands, you just type words. The system figures out what you mean and gives you ranked results.

sections.title: Search and Retrieval Queries
sections.content:
A WAIS search session began with the client sending a Search Request APDU (Application Protocol Data Unit) containing a Type-3 query. This query had two main components: the seed words (plain text entered by the user) and an optional list of document objects for relevance feedback. Each document object included a Doc-ID (document identifier), type, chunk-code, and start/end locations, allowing the server to find similar documents to ones the user found relevant.

The server responded with a Search Response APDU containing WAIS Citations. Each citation included a headline (key words from the document), a relevance rank (numerical score normalized to 1000), a list of available formats (text, PostScript, TIFF, etc.), the Doc-ID, and document length. For document retrieval, the client sent a Type-1 query with up to four terms: the document identifier, the desired format, and optional start/end locations for chunked retrieval. The response contained the requested document or portion in the specified format.
sections.eli5: When you search WAIS, you type words, and it sends back a ranked list of documents with headlines and scores showing how well each matches. If you want to read a document, you can ask for just part of it.

sections.title: Implementation Details
sections.content:
WAIS supported the Init and Search Facilities of Z39.50-1988, using TCP for network transport rather than the OSI presentation services assumed by the Z39.50 standard. The Type-3 query format allowed the client to avoid parsing or understanding Z39.50's complex Attribute system. Each query term could use specific attributes such as use="un" (system-control-number) with relation="re" (equal) for document IDs, use="wt" (data-type) for format selection, and use="wb", "wl", "wp" for byte, line, and paragraph positioning in chunked retrieval.

The preferred message size negotiated during initialization controlled how many WAIS Citations were returned per search response. Because clients had limited receive buffers, especially for full-text documents and images, WAIS designed chunked retrieval as a core feature rather than an afterthought. This design proved essential for practical deployment when moving large multimedia documents across bandwidth-limited 1990s networks.
sections.eli5: WAIS uses special codes to tell the server what kind of search to do (looking for a document ID, a format type, or a byte range). The server and client negotiate how much data to send at once.

sections.title: Purpose and Migration Path
sections.content:
This memo's primary purpose was to initiate discussion for a migration path from Z39.50-1988 to Z39.50-1992 and then to Z39.50-1994 as those standards evolved. The memo was not intended as a detailed implementation specification, but rather a high-level description of WAIS design goals and assumptions that justified its particular use of Z39.50-1988.

The report acknowledges that as Z39.50 evolved, WAIS would need to adapt. Future RFCs would document WAIS implementations of Z39.50-1992 and Z39.50-1994. Over time, many WAIS requirements did feed into subsequent Z39.50 versions as the standard became more general-purpose. The document also references the DOI (Document Identifier) specification, a standard for uniquely identifying documents in electronic form, which complemented WAIS's retrieval mechanism.
sections.eli5: This memo explains how WAIS worked in 1994 and hints that it would upgrade as the Z39.50 standard improved. The goal was to keep WAIS current with international standards rather than drift into obsolescence.
